37009438d78e5f26: RIYADH: The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed four cruise missiles and three drones on Tuesday in the capital Riyadh and the kingdom's south, as Yemen's Houthis pressed on with attacks.
"Three cruise missiles destroyed in the Riyadh and southern areas," coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X, later adding that "two drones intercepted and destroyed" in the same areas.
Minutes later, it said it had intercepted and destroyed another cruise missile targeting Riyadh.
The coalition later reported intercepting and destroying a third drone over Riyadh.
A powerful explosion rang out in the Saudi capital, with a phone alert sent to residents saying that "the city of Riyadh is facing a hostile aerial threat".

While walking down a major avenue in Riyadh, a witness told AFP he "saw a projectile cutting across the sky" above a mall, saying it left "a yellowish trail of light followed by a trail of smoke. Then, we heard an explosion".
"People were calm; no one was speaking. We were scared and all looking up at the sky," he added, requesting anonymity.

Saudi Civil Defence later reported brief alerts warning of a potential danger in Al-Sulayil and Wadi Dawasir, two towns in the southwest of Riyadh province, several hundred kilometres from the capital.
The reported strikes came after the Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, leaving 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.

Maliki announced on Tuesday that the coalition had launched strikes in Yemen's Sanaa and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada, targeting facilities used to "supply the war effort" by the Houthis.

4be26f8fb3f1483b: MADRID: Atletico Madrid eased to a 2-0 win over Manchester United in the Champions League on Tuesday to pile pressure on Red Devils coach Michael Carrick.
Pablo Barrios pounced inside the first minute for Diego Simeone's side and after Leny Yoro's 74th minute red card set United back further, Ademola Lookman added another for the hosts in Madrid.
Man United have made their worst domestic start in 40 years and this league phase defeat in the Spanish capital was another blow, with the team now winless in five games across all competitions.
Man United defender Lisandro Martinez said the team's performance was "really poor" and suggested it was also a reflection of how the club is being run.
"It is annoying, disappointing coming here and I am not seeing my team trying to get an amazing result here, it's disappointing," he told Amazon Prime.
Carrick handed Carlos Baleba his first start for the club since arriving from Brighton this summer, as well as pushing captain Bruno Fernandes out to the right side.

Atletico were without their skipper Koke, after the death of his mother, while coach Simeone selected Julian Alvarez from the off for the first time this season at the Metropolitano stadium, after he tried to force a departure this summer.
"As well as for the team, it was very important (to win) for Koke and all of his family, it's a very tough day for them, this victory is for them," said Barrios.
"Getting the goal so soon helped us to manage the game later, I'm really happy for the win."
Atletico fans ordered their supporters to "defend what we love" with a banner display before kick-off and the Rojiblancos were ahead after just 50 seconds.
Alex Baena found a way in behind United's defence and cut the ball across for Barrios, with Ayden Heaven unable to keep the midfielder's shot from crossing the line.
Barrios held up six fingers to pay tribute to Koke.
"It was really tough news for everyone and I said if I scored I would do that," added Barrios.
Carrick had said it was important to get off to a fast start, but his team were unable to follow his instructions.
Bryan Mbuemo might have equalised for the visitors, nudging the ball through Cristian Romero's legs but firing just wide.
Alejandro Grimaldo came inches away from extending Atletico's lead with a free-kick which hit the angle between post and crossbar.

The hosts thought they had a second when Johnny Cardoso finished neatly from the edge of the box before half-time but the goal was disallowed after a VAR review showed the ball had struck Marcos Llorente's hand during the build-up.
Hitting the woodwork
Alvarez, yet to score this season for Atletico, hit the post early in the second half.
United rallied and Fernandes's lob drifted narrowly wide before the Portuguese playmaker hit the crossbar from the left of the box after a corner routine.
However the three-time European champions suffered a setback when defender Yoro was harshly dismissed after a VAR review for bringing down Canada striker Jonathan David as the last man.

It opened the door for Atletico to grab their second, with David foiled by goalkeeper Senne Lammens but London-born Nigeria international Lookman was on hand to tuck home the rebound after 79 minutes.
Carrick withdrew playmaker Fernandes, looking ahead to the weekend visit to face rivals Leeds in the English top flight, where improvement is badly needed.
"It is very hard to say after a defeat that there is positives. We just have to work hard to keep working and keep trusting in our structure," United midfielder Youri Tielemans told Amazon Prime.
"We have to keep working, keep trusting each other and be together on this."
Atletico goalkeeper Jan Oblak saved from United substitute Matheus Cunha in the final stages but there was no way back for United.
Simeone's side were able to claim their first points after an opening defeat at Liverpool.

5074883411105540: SAN FRANCISCO: A Saudi employee of OpenAI was arrested after an investigation found that they had secretly planted a recording device in one of its San Francisco offices, the tech company and federal prosecutors said on Tuesday.
"We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.
OpenAI's security team found the device late last month, and the employee, a Saudi national, was arrested on Oct 9, the US Justice Department said.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer, had worked for OpenAI since July 2025 and allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room", according to a Justice Department statement.
Alfozan was allegedly caught on camera "near" the conference room multiple times but was not authorised to participate in meetings held there.
He used a "productivity tool" to search for more information about OpenAI's office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people's locations, according to the statement.
A chatbot account connected to his spouse also allegedly contained queries related to remote audio recording and encrypting SD cards.
"This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in the statement.
"The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America's cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats," Clayton added.
The arrest and allegations come amid a fierce global race to dominate the artificial intelligence (AI) market.
Saudi Arabia's state-backed AI firm Humain invested US$3 billion in Elon Musk's xAI shortly before the American billionaire's space company, SpaceX, acquired the AI division in February.
Now known as SpaceXAI, the division announced last year that it was teaming up with Humain to build a 500-megawatt data centre in Saudi Arabia.

5a5f516df00c7b3a: LONDON: Arsenal blew away Lille with a three-goal blitz in seven second-half minutes for a 3-0 win to extend their perfect start to the Champions League.
Jurrien Timber's deft finish opened the floodgates just after the hour at the Emirates Stadium before Eberechi Eze and Bukayo Saka rounded off the scoring.
Victory takes Arsenal into a share of the lead at the top of the Champions League table alongside Barcelona and Sporting Lisbon.
Mikel Arteta was able to use the wealth of resources at his disposal as he made five changes to the side that beat Leeds 2-1 on Saturday.
But it was Lille boss Davide Ancelotti, son of Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti, who was the happier after a goalless first half.
The visitors even had the ball in the net but Ayase Ueda was flagged offside.
Bruno Guimaraes came closest to breaking the deadlock for Arsenal before the break when he fired wide from close range and then his powerful shot from range was parried by Berke Ozer.
The Gunners quickly went through the gears in the second period once Timber dinked the ball over Ozer from Noni Madueke's pass.
Arteta had left arguably his three most potent attacking weapons on the bench and the introduction of Saka, Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard made an immediate impact.
"The ones that finish the game are extraordinary," said Arteta.
"They increase the intensity, the quality and we suffocate them more and more and more."
Saka's low cross picked out Eze whose deflected shot flew into the top corner to end any doubt over the destiny of the three points.
The England winger then finished off an exquisite team move from Havertz's cut-back for Arsenal's third.
There were further cheers from the home fans when Olivier Giroud came on as a late substitute for Lille on his return to the club where he scored 105 goals in a six-year spell.
But Giroud could not conjure up another Emirates goal as Lille remain without a Champions League point after defeat to Real Betis on matchday one.
6469142ae7602b33: NEW YORK: US-based chain CVS Pharmacy has agreed to pay US$315 million to resolve a lawsuit alleging that it filled unlawful opioid prescriptions and engaged in other fraudulent activity, federal prosecutors said on Tuesday.

"Today's settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department's efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfil prescriptions for controlled substances," Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward said in a statement.
The settlement comes after prosecutors alleged that CVS illegally filled prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances between 2013 and 2025, according to the statement.
The complaint also accused CVS of filling prescriptions from "pill mill" prescribers "who issued large numbers of controlled substance prescriptions without any medical purpose".
In a statement, CVS confirmed a settlement with the Justice Department but said it had admitted no wrongdoing, adding: "We strongly disagree with the claims made in this case."
CVS employs more than 27,000 pharmacists at its stores across the United States and said they had implemented "programmes to help our pharmacists make the best decisions on behalf of patients".

The settlement resolves a civil lawsuit filed by whistleblower Hillary Estright, a former CVS employee, under a legal provision "which authorises private parties to sue on behalf of the United States and receive a share of any recovery".
Estright's share of the settlement has not yet been determined.
609563f4c9b80c11: PETALING JAYA: The owners of 86 units in an affordable housing scheme have been ordered to pay damages to a federal agency, after the Johor Bahru High Court ruled their pursuit of additional compensation for late delivery breached a settlement agreement already in place.

Justice Wong Mee Ling, in allowing Perbadanan Perumahan Rakyat 1Malaysia’s (PR1MA) counterclaim, ordered each unit owner in Residensi Prima Tebrau to pay the agency nominal damages of RM10,000, together with RM5,000 in costs.

The owners had previously entered into a settlement agreement with PR1MA for liquidated ascertained damages (LAD), and had received payment in full, but brought the suit seeking additional compensation for late delivery of their units.

In a ruling delivered last week, Wong said that once parties have fully performed the terms of an agreement and accepted its benefits, they cannot readily refile or depart from the compromise reached.
“The (signed) letter of acceptance constitutes a binding compromise under Section 64 of the Contract Act 1950,” she said.
“By accepting the settlement sum, these plaintiffs (the unit owners) entered into accord and satisfaction, which effectively discharged the defendant (PR1MA) from further liability.”
To allow the unit owners to pursue their claim after “pocketing the benefits” would constitute unjust enrichment, she added.

Wong also dismissed LAD claims by the owners of seven units who were not parties to the settlement agreement, stating they were time-barred under the Limitations Act 1953. They were also ordered to pay costs of RM5,000 each.
The case before Wong involved the determination of six questions of law posed by the parties to the court.

The dispute stemmed from statutory sale and purchase agreements (SPAs) entered into by PR1MA and the unit owners between 2012 and 2015, which stipulated a 54‑month completion period for the delivery of vacant possession and common facilities, instead of the usual 36 months.

The suit, brought in 2021, was predicated on the argument that the completion period had been illegally extended by the controller of housing and should revert to 36 months, as provided for under the Housing Developers (Control and Licensing) Regulations 1989.
Wong ruled that the extension of the time for completion of the housing project granted by the controller was valid and binding on purchasers despite a subsequent change in the law.

“Accordingly, the 54-month (completion) period stipulated in the SPA remains valid and enforceable. The plaintiff's attempt to retrospectively substitute that period with a 36-month period is therefore legally unacceptable,” said Wong.

The judge also held that because the cause of action for all the unit owners accrued at the execution of their respective SPAs, the six-year limitation period prescribed by law “served as a universal bar to their claims”.
NG Vinod appeared for the unit owners, while Shahrysham Kamran and Danish Abdul Rasid appeared for PR1MA.
b1bf5a18442ce741: PETALING JAYA: Pemilik 86 unit skim perumahan mampu milik diperintah membayar ganti rugi kepada sebuah agensi persekutuan selepas Mahkamah Tinggi Johor Bahru memutuskan tuntutan bagi pampasan tambahan berhubung kelewatan penyerahan melanggar perjanjian penyelesaian sedia ada.

Hakim Wong Mee Ling dalam membenarkan tuntutan balas Perbadanan Perumahan Rakyat 1Malaysia (PR1MA), memerintahkan setiap pemilik unit di Residensi Prima Tebrau membayar ganti rugi nominal RM10,000 kepada agensi itu berserta kos RM5,000.

Pemilik berkenaan sebelum ini memeterai perjanjian penyelesaian dengan PR1MA bagi ganti rugi ditetapkan (LAD) dan telah menerima bayaran penuh, namun bertindak memfailkan saman bagi menuntut pampasan tambahan atas kelewatan penyerahan unit mereka.

Dalam keputusan minggu lalu, Wong berkata sebaik sahaja pihak terlibat melaksanakan sepenuhnya terma perjanjian dan menerima faedahnya, mereka tidak boleh sewenang-wenangnya menarik balik atau menyimpang daripada kompromi yang telah dicapai.
“Surat penerimaan yang (sudah ditandatangani) tersebut membentuk kompromi yang mengikat di bawah Seksyen 64 Akta Kontrak 1950,” katanya.

“Dengan menerima jumlah penyelesaian itu, pihak-pihak plaintif ini (pemilik unit) telah mementerai persetujuan dan pelunasan yang secara efektif melepaskan pihak defendan (PR1MA) daripada liabiliti selanjutnya.”
Tindakan membenarkan pemilik unit meneruskan tuntutan mereka selepas 'menerima dan menikmati faedah berkenaan' akan membawa kepada pengayaan tanpa hak, kata hakim.

Wong turut menolak tuntutan LAD oleh pemilik tujuh unit yang bukan sebahagian daripada perjanjian penyelesaian tersebut, dengan menyatakan tuntutan mereka dikekang tempoh had masa di bawah Akta Had Masa 1953. Mereka juga diperintahkan membayar kos RM5,000 setiap seorang.
Kes di hadapan Wong melibatkan penentuan enam persoalan undang-undang yang dikemukakan pihak-pihak yang bertikai.

Pertikaian itu berpunca daripada perjanjian jual beli (SPA) berkanun dimeterai PR1MA dengan pemilik unit antara 2012 hingga 2015, yang menetapkan tempoh penyiapan selama 54 bulan bagi penyerahan pemilikan kosong dan kemudahan bersama, berbanding tempoh lazim 36 bulan.

Saman difailkan pada 2021 tersebut diasaskan atas hujahan bahawa tempoh penyiapan berkenaan telah dilanjutkan secara tidak sah oleh pengawal perumahan dan sepatutnya dikembalikan kepada 36 bulan, seperti diperuntukkan di bawah Peraturan-peraturan Pemajuan Perumahan (Kawalan dan Pelesenan) 1989.
Wong memutuskan bahawa lanjutan tempoh penyiapan projek perumahan diluluskan pengawal adalah sah dan mengikat pembeli walaupun terdapat perubahan undang-undang selepas itu.

“Justeru, tempoh (penyiapan) 54 bulan ditetapkan dalam SPA kekal sah dan boleh dikuat kuasa. Percubaan plaintif untuk menggantikan tempoh tersebut secara retrospektif dengan tempoh 36 bulan tidak boleh diterima dari sudut undang-undang,” kata Wong.
NG Vinod bertindak bagi pihak pemilik unit, manakala Shahrysham Kamran dan Danish Abdul Rasid mewakili PR1MA.
7f2a3bb0ce96e8e2: STAVANGER: Bayern Munich were held 3-3 at Viking in the Champions League on Tuesday with the Norwegian champions equalising late through Herman Haugen after Michael Olise was sent off.
Bayern trailed 2-0 at halftime thanks to goals from Gianni Stensness and Peter Christiansen.

Bayern concede early again

With just 72 seconds gone, Stensness headed in an outswinging corner to give the hosts a shock lead.
Bayern ramped up the pressure but could not break through, with Kane twice heading into the waiting arms of Viking goalie Arild Ostbo.
Not content to absorb Bayern pressure and cling to a narrow lead, Viking launched a lightning-fast counter-attack and doubled their advantage after 38 minutes.
Top goalscorer Christiansen finished off a slick move to give Viking a 2-0 lead.
Bayern were handed a lifeline when Konrad Laimer was felled in the box just after the break, bringing Kane to the spot.
After a stuttering run up, the 33-year-old guided the ball into the bottom right of the goal, past the fingertips of Ostbo.
On the hour, Kane shed his marker and headed in a Joshua Kimmich cross to lock up the scores.
Diaz had an effort ruled out for offside just a minute later but the Colombian was the beneficiary of a brilliant Kane chip 10 minutes on.
Kane lofted a ball to Laimer, whose saved shot rebounded cleanly into Diaz's path.
The England captain appeared to have saved Bayern, until Olise was sent from the pitch.

The France winger saw yellow for a foul and then picked up another when he threw the ball directly at Viking captain Zlatko Tripic's face right in front of the referee, leaving Bayern a man down with 16 minutes left.
Viking pushed and Haugen headed in at the far post in the 90th minute to snatch the hosts a memorable draw.

379dbb8dacf45ae1: LOS ANGELES: Duane Davis, the former Los Angeles gang leader who boasted in books and interviews of his involvement in the killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, only to deny it when he came to trial, was sentenced to a minimum 40 years in prison on Tuesday.

"You don't get to take a man from his family. You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur," Judge Carli Kierny told a Las Vegas court as she handed down the 40-years-to-life sentence.
Shakur was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting the US East Coast against the West Coast and was just 25 when he was gunned down in Las Vegas.

A trial heard how Davis, the one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips, ordered the Sept 7, 1996 killing of the hip-hop artist after his own nephew had been beaten by members of Shakur's entourage at a Las Vegas casino.

About two hours after the casino confrontation, the "California Love" artist was shot by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was riding in the front passenger seat.
Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later.
Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.
3cf6d4460fee3217: ROME: Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation on Tuesday and "woke up normally" after the procedure, the Vatican said.
A Vatican source said further tests were being carried out to determine whether the cancer had spread.
"To ensure the procedure was radical, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed," the Vatican said in a statement.
The operation "confirmed the diagnosis of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the pre-operative tests", it said.
The 71-year-old pope was in the operating room at Rome's Gemelli hospital for a total of three hours, with the operation lasting half that time.
"The surgery was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said, with a source adding that he had requested dinner after the procedure.
Juanita Mora, medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, told AFP that when this type of cancer is "caught in early stages, then it has a very, very good prognosis".
She said much would depend on the stage of the cancer found and whether it had spread.
In cases of surgical removal, when the cancer is caught early and localised, five-year survival rates for lung adenocarcinoma were "80 to 98 per cent", she said.
"They'll determine if he needs chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy for the adenocarcinoma," she said.
'I will pray a lot'
Leo had entered the hospital smiling and waving earlier on Tuesday, hours before the surgery.
He will be staying in a room on the 10th floor of the building, next to a papal suite with a private chapel that is currently under renovation.
The Vatican has said it expects his recovery to take a week.
His audiences have been cancelled until October 20, and the operation raises questions about whether the pope will go on a lengthy visit to Latin America next month.
The surgery marks Leo's first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on May 8, 2025.
In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in St Peter's Square that doctors had discovered a nodule "at a very early stage" during medical checks.
"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene," he said.

The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo's predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments.
Ahead of the operation, people outside the hospital expressed concern over the pope's condition.
Giorgia Fei, a 57-year-old Italian, said she had been worried.
"However, the Holy Father is in very good hands here at the hospital because we have some outstanding doctors," she said.
"I will pray a lot for him."
Giuseppe Purpura, 72, said he too was concerned.
"He's still quite young and I really wasn't expecting this. I thought he was in better health," he said, noting that "thankfully it was caught in time".

The Vicar General for the Diocese of Rome, Cardinal Baldassare Reina, led a rosary prayer for the pope inside the hospital chapel, which was broadcast by the Vatican. Dozens of people attended, and Reina asked all the city's parishes to join in.
The Vatican secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, told ANSA news agency that Leo had been "very calm" about his condition when they met on Monday.
The Vatican told AFP the nodule was found during routine health checks and that there were no symptoms that led to the pope's lungs being examined.
Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health.
He is scheduled to travel to South America from November 6 to 17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd
9983fac4e201e9e6: WASHINGTON: The US treasury department said Tuesday that it is imposing penalties of more than US$1.2 billion on Bank of America, citing "violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws."
The second biggest US bank failed to properly report more than US$5 billion in "suspicious transactions," the department said.

Some of these involved risks related to national security and other concerns, including transactions "indicative of Chinese money laundering networks" and illicit finance around the southwest US border.

The overall charge involves US$1.2 billion assessed by the treasury department's financial crimes enforcement network. This includes a US$750 million civil penalty from a key bank regulator, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

The treasury's office of foreign assets control also announced a US$11.6 million settlement with the bank over "apparent violations of numerous sanctions programmes, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism."
"Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law," said US treasury secretary Scott Bessent in a statement.

"When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks," he said.
The announcement marks a hit to Bank of America just a day before it reports its third-quarter earnings.
A Bank of America spokesperson told AFP its results would include a US$1.2 billion charge weighing on net income by around 17 cents per share.
They added that the institution is committed to finishing the work needed to address issues that regulators raised.
"We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement across thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activity reports each year," the spokesperson said.
US regulators have published a consent order requiring Bank of America to work with a third party to identify and report suspicious transactions that went undetected.
The institution will also have to undergo an independent review of its programs for monitoring suspicious activity, and on other forms of due diligence.
The bank is subject to a December 2024 cease-and-desist order as well, calling for it to address issues in its anti-money laundering program and compliance with the Bank Secrecy Act.
But the treasury noted Tuesday that the bank "failed to prioritise" compliance despite agreeing to the 2024 order.

Due to Bank of America's "egregious and continued" violations of the Bank Secrecy Act, the OCC imposed its biggest civil money penalty assessed against a bank, said comptroller of the currency Jonathan Gould.
Bank of America shares were down 2.6% in after-hours trading, following the Treasury's announcement.
f81bfc1279a770ca: ALOR SETAR: Tiga remaja lelaki cedera akibat terkena renjatan elektrik selepas bendera dibawa semasa perarakan tokong sayur di Mergong, malam tadi dipercayai terkena talian pencawang elektrik bervoltan tinggi.

Setiausaha Persatuan Tokong Sayur Mergong, Chah Boon Chuan, berkata kejadian kira-kira 9 malam itu mengakibatkan dua mangsa berusia 17 tahun dan seorang lagi yang berusia 16 tahun dikejarkan ke Hospital Sultanah Bahiyah (HSB).

“Kejadian berlaku ketika ribuan peserta perarakan sedang berarak di jalan utama di kawasan berkenaan sebelum satu bendera dipercayai terkena talian elektrik. Bendera itu ditiup angin kencang ketika hujan rintik sebelum disyaki terkena pada talian elektrik.

“Seorang remaja yang memegang bendera serta dua lagi yang berada berhampiran cedera akibat terkena renjatan elektrik. Ketiga-tiga mereka difahamkan sedang dirawat di zon merah HSB,” katanya ketika ditemui di pekarangan Jabatan Kecemasan dan Trauma HSB, malam tadi.
Beliau berkata, tiga remaja itu masih menerima rawatan dan keadaan terkini mereka belum diketahui.
“Batang bendera yang digunakan untuk membawa bendera itu diperbuat daripada buluh dan ini merupakan kejadian pertama berlaku,” katanya.
Terdahulu, tular beberapa video di laman media sosial mengenai kejadian itu termasuk keadaan mangsa yang terbaring di atas jalan.
4a900c09b17d3330: MILAN: Club Brugge and their young forward Nicolo Tresoldi shocked Inter Milan 4-3 in the Champions League on Tuesday.
Tresoldi, a 22-year-old Italian-German forward, scored the first three goals for the Belgian side.
Former Inter goalkeeper Yann Sommer returned to the San Siro in the Brugge goal.
And the Swiss keeper denied Lautaro Martinez after ten minutes with Marcus Thuram firing wide early on.
A Hakan Calhanoglu foul on Carlos Forbs resulted in a penalty which Tresoldi slotted in just before the half hour.

Tresoldi picked up his second after capitalising on a goalkeeping blunder by the Inter keeper just after the hour and reacting faster than the Inter defence for the third with a quarter of an hour to go.
"It was an unbelievable and fantastic night. I dreamt many times of these nights and this was the best dream," said Tresoldi.
Martinez had given his team a lifeline just before the break following a move initiated by Thuram followed by a Federico Dimarco backheel assist.

For weeks on end, parts of Indonesian Borneo have resembled an Armageddon landscape with masked residents immersed in a putrid, red-brown haze as wildfires devour peatlands near homes and farms.

Burning slowly, mostly under the surface and sometimes for months on end, peatland fires are responsible for much of the dry season haze that this year has tainted air as far afield as Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines.
Peatlands are composed of organic material that does not completely decompose in water-logged conditions and has settled over thousands of years into a layered soil-like substance.
Healthy peatlands are home to diverse plants and trees like nutmeg and durian, and animals that can include endangered orangutans, clouded leopards, Sumatran tigers, sun bears and tapirs.
They are porous and absorbent, making them critical for flood containment.
While they cover only about three per cent of global land, peatlands store about a third of the world's soil carbon — double that trapped by forests.
Indonesia has the world's biggest share of tropical peatland, about a third of the global total.
Of Indonesia's estimated 24.2 million hectares of peatland, 16.4 million hectares have been degraded and are vulnerable to fire, according to the Pantau Gambut non-governmental organisation.
The culprit is mainly industrial-scale plantations for timber, pulp and paper, padi and palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world's biggest producer by far.
To cultivate peatlands, they are drained with canal networks that in Indonesia span about 285,000km, according to Pantau Gambut research — seven times the circumference of Earth.
The water runs into rivers or the sea, leaving the dried-out peatlands vulnerable to burning, especially in strong El Nino years that can bring severe drought to Indonesia.
Peatland fires are often imperceptible but for the foul smoke they emit and the heat they generate underfoot.
The many layers of thick carbon can keep smouldering in "zombie fires" for weeks, and are hard to put out.
While less than a third of wildfires in Indonesia are on peatlands, they produce most of the haze, according to Greenpeace research.
This toxic smog contains harmful elements, including formaldehyde, hydrogen cyanide and ammonia, as well as PM2.5 particles small enough to penetrate the lungs or bloodstream.
The World Health Organisation has linked PM2.5 exposure to increased illness and death.
By Oct 6, Indonesian wildfires had emitted 140.5 megatonnes of planet-warming carbon, around 13 per cent of the global total this year, according to the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.

1caa10fc6fdb6473: SAN FRANCISCO: Small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help, AI giant Anthropic said.
The finding potentially opens a new front in the cybersecurity threats emerging from AI, which have rattled governments and the companies rushing to adopt the technology.

The research, posted on an Anthropic blog late Monday, comes as tech companies race to build ever more powerful AI directly into phones, laptops, cars and household devices, rather than running it only in distant data centres.
A computer worm is malicious software that spreads between machines on its own. Researchers at Anthropic said an AI version would no longer need powerful data centres to operate.
Instead, it could hop from device to device across networks of cheap, poorly secured consumer hardware such as smart TV boxes and kitchen appliances.

The researchers based their calculations of how far such a worm could spread on Kimwolf, a botnet - a network of hijacked devices controlled by hackers - that infected more than two million devices at its peak, mostly off-brand Android TV boxes.

An AI worm of the kind described in the research would likely be slow, taking days to copy itself, William Zhou and Daniel Freeman of Anthropic said, comparing it to a slowly multiplying swarm of fruit flies.
Once created, it would be hard to stamp out, because there would be no central switch to turn off.
Anthropic’s researchers said their estimate of how fast and how far AI-fuelled malware could spread was rough, since it was based on one type of gadget and one past botnet.

But over time, the amount of computing power sitting in everyday gadgets is expected to keep growing, while the AI models needed to pull this off are likely to keep getting smaller, the researchers added.

Varun Chandrasekaran, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Illinois, said the research was unsurprising and matched similar recent findings, though he cautioned that Anthropic’s work had not been independently verified.
He also noted that security on devices like thermostats or home cameras "has historically been very weak."
But when it came to AI, the biggest current threat was human bad actors using artificial intelligence to sharpen their hacks, rather than AI systems themselves going rogue, he said.
"A malicious human being is now supercharged with AI to perform bad things and we are seeing this happen at scale," he added.

The rogue AI debate came to the fore in July, when AI programs running on OpenAI models escaped an internal company test and broke into the systems of AI platform Hugging Face - apparently hunting for the test's answers.
The incident and subsequent reports like it have sparked international pressure for closer regulation of AI, even as the Trump administration resists the idea and urges the industry to police itself.

Anthropic and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI have been accused by powerful voices in the White House and Silicon Valley of stoking fears about AI and encouraging government rules in order to protect their market dominance from smaller rivals.

Brad Smith, OpenAI investor Microsoft's president, warned Tuesday that industry and governments must "act with urgency" to create "real and effective safety standards" in order to rein in the risks of artificial intelligence.

758478a3d7511684: ISTANBUL: Barcelona and Lamine Yamal rediscovered their sparkle after a rocky first-half spell in the cauldron of Istanbul's Ali Sami Yen stadium to win 4-1 away to Galatasaray in the Champions League on Tuesday.

39c4f5fe4505a1b3: PARIS: Tens of thousands of people joined rallies across France on Tuesday to support protesting high school students demanding better conditions in a major challenge to president Emmanuel Macron as his term winds down.
Some 161,500 people turned out in the rallies, according to the interior ministry - more than double the 71,500 estimate it gave for demonstrations on Thursday last week.
Although most of the demonstrations were peaceful, violence erupted on the sidelines of one of two Paris marches that the interior ministry said drew 41,500 people.

AFP journalists saw some cars set on fire and police fired tear gas in the Invalides square as masked youths tried to erect barricades across roads and threw objects. Tear gas was also fired during a demonstration in Lyon.
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg took part in one demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. She said she had joined the protests because "our future is being robbed".

French unions said 480,000 people took part in the rallies and the numbers suggested increased street opposition to the government just six months before a vote for a successor to Macron, who is completing his maximum second mandate.

The latest agitation came as the centrist government launched a debate in parliament on a cost-cutting budget, facing fierce opposition from the left and right, while France's worsening debt has spooked the bond market.
Pressure will increase as on Saturday national demonstrations against the cost of living are to take place, and unions and student groups see the two protest currents merging.
The students have been given strong backing by the far-left opposition France Unbowed (LFI) party whose leader and presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon was seen among crowds in Paris.
Dialogue, 'not repression'
Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police and AFP reporters.
"We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression," said 16-year-old Emeline, outside a Marseille school.
"We're here because we really feel we're not being heard by the government," said Nina, 17.
The student movement sprang up last month at lycees - high schools for those aged 15 to 18 - with students blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.
Perceived heavy-handed police action against the students drove many to join Tuesday's demonstrations.
One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a teargas canister in his face.

Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of violence against demonstrators, according to interior minister Laurent Nunez who said nearly 900 police had suffered injuries during the protests.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured, the education ministry said.
'Not budging'

"We're not giving up the fight, whether it's for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence," said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.
Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved.
"Initially we were terrified," said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife.
"We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then."
France's education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed Tuesday.
University student union l'Union Etudiante reported 90% of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.
They have dismissed a government pledge - made after last week's demonstrations - to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools.
"We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging," said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.
On Monday, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues "deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect".

40ca599c6d501c62: ROME: Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous growth removed from his right lung in a 90-minute operation on Tuesday and "woke up normally" after the procedure, the Vatican said.

"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene," he said.

Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and believed to generally be in good health.
He is scheduled to travel to South America from Nov 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
It was not immediately clear what would happen if the pope was forced into a longer recovery.

Under Church law, a figure known as the Cardinal Camerlengo - or chamberlain - takes over administrative duties if the pope dies, but pontiffs do not have a deputy to replace them if they become incapacitated.

238861a86740711f: KINSHASA: The worst Ebola outbreak ever in the Democratic Republic of Congo has passed the 9,000-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,000 since early October, health authorities said Tuesday.

Initial doses of the Ervebo vaccine, whose effectiveness has been proven against the Zaire strain - the most common variant in the past - have been administered in recent weeks to frontline volunteers as part of a clinical trial.
A clinical trial for an Ebola vaccine is expected to be launched in the DRC before the end of the month, experts from the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Tuesday.
11e83311a7c54e72: As artificial intelligence becomes more and more powerful, its ability to handle human-like tasks is undeniable. Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language, or write computer code. Like the brain’s circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance. The question for many neuroscientists is: What can these machine systems teach them about how the brain learns? And what kinds of models are likely to be the most informative? In a paper published Oct. 9 in the journal PNAS, scientists at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research and K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network’s approach to learning is the network’s ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer. They show that it is possible for an artificial neural network to build its own learning machinery. With some simple instructions about how and when connections should change, a group of randomly connected units can reshape itself into an effective information-processing network, learning from the data it is trained on. Biological learning “Current AI technology is working very well, but it doesn’t necessarily use a learning algorithm that is used by the brain,” says Qianli Liao, a K. Lisa Yang ICoN Center Postdoctoral Fellow in the labs of MIT professors and McGovern Institure members Tomaso Poggio and Mark Harnett, and co-first author of the PNAS paper with MIT Research Scientist Liu Ziyin and graduate student Yulu Gan. Liao explains that engineers design the rules about how connections change as an artificial neural network processes training data and receives feedback about its mistakes.   When it comes to training AI to do its job, the approach is powerful. But Liao and his colleagues caution that networks designed in this way may not offer much insight into biological learning. “The brain doesn't have an external designer or architect,” Liao says. “The brain has to organize itself. And we need to know how simple rules are going to make the brain organize.” The rules that reshape neural connections as an animal learns may be different in different parts of the brain, or they may change as the brain becomes more mature. Neuroscientists are working to understand how those rules work and how they might be disrupted by aging or disease — a vital step toward developing new therapies and prevention strategies. Liao points to the development of brain-computer interfaces, which aim to restore communication when the brain’s language abilities are lost or let paralyzed patients control neuroprosthetic limbs, as one potential application. “None of these can work without knowing the rules behind neuron-neuron interactions,” he says. “That’s not achievable by just designing a circuit that works very well.” An artificial neural network’s value to neuroscience should instead be judged by the extent to which it can organize itself — not just its connections, but also the machinery that adjusts those connections. Self-organized artificial learning Working with Poggio and Hartnett, Liao, Ziyin, and Gan set out to develop and validate a self-organizing computational network capable of learning. Liao explained that the network’s structure begins with multiple layers of randomly interconnected neuron-like units. Within each layer, every neuron-like component is subject to the same rules about how connections should be adjusted. “They just interact with each other using that rule, and they develop some type of behavior,” he says. The team’s network implements the kind of simple rules thought to rewire brain circuits as humans and other animals learn from their experiences. In both the brain and the machine network, for example, “neurons that fire together wire together.” In other words, when two connected neurons are activated at the same time, the connection between them strengthens.  The team showed that a self-organizing network governed by rules like these can learn to recognize patterns and classify images. They explain that in their model, learning is enabled by self-assembling motifs that emerge according to simple rules, then serve as building blocks for functional circuits. As their network learned, these motifs reorganized themselves using an optimization strategy similar to the approach built into most modern machine learning systems, called gradient descent, in which connections are gradually adjusted in response to errors in order to improve performance. Most modern AI implements gradient descent through some form of the back-propagation algorithm, which neuroscientists say is unlikely to be used by the brain. The team compared its self-organizing network to networks designed to learn in this way and found that it performed at a similar level. Connecting brains and machines Poggio says finding a biological parallel to back-propagation could trigger significant progress in both AI and neuroscience.  “If the synaptic motifs we propose are, in fact, used by the brain to do what backpropagation does for artificial neural networks, then we will have a strong connection at the level of fundamental mechanisms between artificial and natural networks — between machines and brains,” he says. Liao says a self-organizing network does not necessarily learn the same way the brain does — but it’s a critical starting point for biological plausibility.  “Self-organization is the first high-level framework,” he says. “Once we are good with self-organization as a measure, then we can talk about next thing.” While the group’s main objective is better understanding the brain, Liao says that knowledge could ultimately improve machine learning systems, too, enabling engineers to develop networks that perform better or in more human-like ways.

8ad1969e4f569b40: MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosted the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB) on Sept. 3, for a stop on its national roadshow. The event convened representatives of state organizations, defense centers, universities, technology companies, and business executives to discuss how Massachusetts' biotechnology ecosystem can strengthen national biodefense capabilities. "We have a lot to leverage in this region to advance biotechnology," said Christina Rudzinski, assistant head of the Biotechnology and Human Systems Division at Lincoln Laboratory. "Many people are already working together to push the bioindustrial sector beyond biopharmaceuticals and into a broader ecosystem across industries. This synergy is where NSCEB comes in — connecting policy to the real-world work already happening, including here at Lincoln Laboratory and across the state." Biotechnology touches many economic and defense sectors, from disease-resistant crops and lifesaving medicines to biofuels and advanced manufacturing materials. In 2022, Congress established the NSCEB to study the national security implications of this rapidly advancing field and issue policy recommendations to ensure continued U.S. leadership.  In April 2025, the 11-member bipartisan and bicameral commission released its report, calling for a minimum of $15 billion in federal investment over five years. According to the report, China is investing aggressively to dominate the field, echoing a pattern the United States has seen before in sectors such as semiconductors. "The coalition of stakeholders working in the Massachusetts biotech ecosystem illustrates how collaborative regional work will help keep the U.S. in the lead by producing exceptional innovation across all areas of biotechnology," said NSCEB Executive Director Caitlin Frazer.  Now in the final year of its three-year mandate, NSCEB is touring the country to see local biotechnology ecosystems in action. The commission will bring insights back to Washington to help members of Congress support their regions' strengths.  Advancing Massachusetts as a defense-biotechnology hub Massachusetts has identified biotechnology as a priority technology area under its Strategic Hub for Innovation, Exchange, and Leadership in Defense (SHIELD) initiative. Launched by Governor Maura Healey in October 2025 alongside $47 million of initial aligned investment, the initiative has moved with speed and at scale. This includes standing up the BioNexus program that leverages state matching funds to develop biotechnology and biomanufacturing solutions for the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM). Further, Healey included a $100 million authorization for defense sector capital projects in the Mass Wins Act, an economic development bill filed in April. The bill is currently being considered by the state legislature. During the roadshow event, Ben Linville-Engler, who co-chairs the SHIELD Working Group and serves as deputy director of the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative, led a panel discussion with representatives from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Business Executives for National Security, Activate, DEVCOM Soldier Center, MassChallenge, Perimeter, Center for Advanced Manufacturing, and the Massachusetts AI Hub. They are among more than 40 partner organizations participating in SHIELD.  "There is incredible convergence between economic development and national security in all domains — land, air, sea, space, cyber, and bio," said Linville-Engler, citing the state's $48.6 billion in defense-sector economic contributions last year. "Massachusetts is committed to biotechnology and national security, and not just in Boston and Cambridge but across the entire state." In July, the SHIELD Working Group submitted a report outlining steps to speed the transition of technology into deployable capabilities, strengthen the defense workforce pipeline, and reinforce the state's national security industrial base.  Lincoln Laboratory is well positioned to support these priorities. As a Department of War federally funded R&D center, the laboratory has deep knowledge of national security needs and sustained ties to academic, commercial, and U.S. government laboratories. "These attributes can help strengthen biotechnology collaborations and integrate and transition solutions across Massachusetts and New England," Rudzinski said. Scaling up biomanufacturing One project advancing this vision is the Biotechnology Scale-up Hub for Innovation, Economic Development, Labor Training, and Defense (BioSHIELD). Planned for Worcester, Massachusetts, this 200,000-square-foot biomanufacturing facility is designed to mobilize the region's defense-biotechnology sector. "BioSHIELD's mission is to accelerate breakthrough biomanufacturing solutions that strengthen national resilience, support commercial innovation, and grow the regional economy," said Edward Wack, project co-lead and principal staff in the laboratory's Biotechnology and Human Systems Division. 6533a9013f8d2d73: In an effort to give its employees better access to GPU resources for inference tasks, Apple has rounded up its Minions, not the animated yellow creatures, but a distributed system that puts idle GPUs across its Macs to work on AI workloads. Apple researchers describe it as "a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads." Apple's researchers said the company has used Minions to make GPU compute more readily available to its teams. "Prior to its adoption, some inference jobs experienced queue times exceeding ten hours due to limited centralized GPU availability," the paper on Minions explains. "With Minions, tasks can often begin execution within minutes by leveraging idle macOS devices." Apple's recently released Mac mini and Mac Studio support clustering using RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) over Thunderbolt 5, allowing compute and memory to be combined to support a single AI workload. This allows, for example, loading a model too large for a single machine to accommodate. Minions is designed to create a virtual GPU cloud from connected Mac hardware to create a fault-tolerant pool of inference workers in a shared distributed inference platform. So instead of sitting idle, GPU resources can be used more readily by teams on the network. It's not necessarily intended as a way to run large models as much as it is to redistribute idle resources on the network. Minions has four primary components: Minion Server, PostgreSQL Metadata Store, Minion Executor, and Minion Watchdog. The Minion Server provides the coordination layer, receiving user requests and making them available as subtasks. The Minion Executor runs inference tasks on a Mac's GPU, uploads the results to S3, and reports execution status through the Minion Server, which maintains task metadata in PostgreSQL. And the Minion Watchdog monitors this process for failures – like one of the Macs in the network not responding – and re-assigns tasks if needed. Database stats get fed to Grafana-based dashboards for real-time visibility. Apple's approach, which focuses on hardware availability and utilization, is not the same as an Nvidia cluster, which focuses on throughput, latency, and efficient GPU utilization for large models. ®

de2574ffe05a1c8f: Nothing sells AI products as well as fear. Using new research, Anthropic claims that self-replicating AI worms could be just months away from spreading across vulnerable IoT devices, which would be a problem if it came true. The frontier lab published a research report Monday suggesting that AI models could eventually self-replicate without relying on datacenter hardware, with a 9-billion-parameter model successfully setting up inference on eight of the nine hardware types Anthropic tested. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off,” Anthropic warned, adding that such an AI worm could also suss out the workings of unfamiliar devices, potentially making it more adaptable than conventional botnets like Mirai, Kimwolf (the representative IoT botnet threat model used in the study), and others. Anthropic’s researchers managed to get a distributed instance of Gemma4-26B-A4B running across 15 generic Android set-top streaming boxes - a common target of traditional botnet malware due to their lax security. Once up and running, the distributed Gemma4 model was able to conduct inference tasks at a blistering 0.39 tokens per second. That, says Anthropic, proves that AI models can conduct inference with their various layers distributed across cheap hardware, but it doesn't prove such a model could self-replicate. For that, the researchers turned to Z.ai’s GLM 5.2. GLM was used to propagate a copy of Llama3.1-8B across eight Google Cloud instances running an Android 15 emulator in a virtual private cloud, which Anthropic said it was able to do with a high degree of success, with the model successfully spreading to all eight nodes in four out of five trials, and seven of eight in the other. “It appears that GLM-5.2 is able to propagate Llama3.1-8B well, which suggests that future small models of the same capability level could also complete the network enumeration, payload delivery, and inference standup steps of the replication process,” Anthropic explained. Sanity check: This isn’t going to end the world, either Frontier AI labs have become adept at publishing findings that portend doom that only they can prevent. Doing more than a cursory reading of this report suggests that this threat is just as deserving of a big, honking asterisk as the rest. Take, for example, what is needed for an AI model to exploit vulnerabilities and spread to various systems. One would think that such an element would be an important part of demonstrating the danger of a self-replicating AI botnet, but Anthropic decided it didn’t need to worry about that for this study. “We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process, since earlier papers CyberGym, ExploitBench, and adaptive worms already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools,” Anthropic explained in the writeup. In other words, the replication these models managed to achieve was done on nodes that were custom-built for this project and deliberately left open to attack, although the draggingly slow inference demonstration ran on real, inexpensive Android TV boxes. As Anthropic notes, AI models can also benefit from being given the right tools to turn them into capable cyberattack agents. There was a custom-built harness called Memento involved in this scenario too. Are IoT nodes that get hijacked by botnets famously insecure? Yes, but it doesn’t take much to prevent the most common ingress routes – that’s just good security hygiene that has nothing to do with the involvement of AI. Anthropic acknowledged that its deliberately simplified exploitation tests provided “an upper bound on real-world success.” Then there’s the aforementioned speed. Anthropic says such AI worms would be challenging to shut down, but estimates that they might take days to double in size. When Mirai appeared on the scene in 2016, it was doubling in around an hour. Anthropic points out that speed is a factor in detection and mitigation, too. AI models are not simple malware packages: They’re massive things that would eat up tons of bandwidth and quickly point to their sources. As an AI botnet grew, that traffic could become more noticeable, making infected devices easier to detect. Finally, end-to-end replication may have been successful with GLM-5.2, but that’s it. Anthropic tested other open-weight models, and they all “fail[ed] reliably,” according to the report. Anthropic didn’t mention how many models it tested. The report also mentions that GLM’s unique success has another important condition: It assumes its capabilities “could be packed into Llama3.1-8B,” stacking another assumption onto this latest house of doomsaying AI cards. “Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end,” Anthropic said, while noting that GLM-5.2 was capable of end-to-end replication, conveniently leaving out all the important caveats. Anthropic further admits that it has no idea "exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take,” or when it might arise, if ever. “If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year,” the company added – again imposing an essential condition on this supposed threat. “As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control,” the company said at the end of its report. “We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.” Here to stay for a given value of not existing yet, of course. Yet again, a frontier lab is warning us of a threat that doesn’t exist yet – at least in this case, basic security measures could make life harder for any future AI-powered botnet. ®

1f62d11b47df3600: A financial analyst is questioning whether the collapse in AI costs owing to the arrival of Chinese, low-cost and open source models will cause a “reset” in the AI story as cloud providers struggle to recoup trillions of dollars of capital spending. In a recent research note focused on Asian markets, Jefferies estimates that about half of the roughly $2.3 trillion contracted backlog at Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Oracle is owned by OpenAI and Anthropic. Yet Chinese AI models, open source/weight and small language models, threaten to undercut the prices the two US leaders charge, casting doubt on their future revenue. Jefferies points to research from global aggregator platform OpenRouter, which found Chinese models processed 76.12 trillion tokens in the week ended 27 September, up from just 4.37 trillion in late April. The top four US providers processed 14.2 trillion tokens. Meanwhile, the launch of Moonshot AI’s open source Kimi K3 is “competing at the frontier” with an estimated 95 percent of the performance of Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5. “The question now is whether all of the above has been priced fully into markets. This writer does not think so,” the Jefferies paper states. The largest hyperscalers are set to collectively spend between $600 and $800 billion this year on building datacenters, funding it increasingly with debt rather than cash. Jefferies, however, questions where the hyperscalers' future revenue streams will come from. “It can no longer be assumed, most particularly with the arrival of the likes of Kimi K3, that large language models will ever be profitable given the related ongoing collapse in token pricing. This is extremely relevant for the hyperscalers since they have invested in datacenter capacity on the assumption that the compute will be purchased by the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI,” the paper says. While the long term bet on AI may be sound, in the medium term, there is a lot of uncertainty, it argues. “The AI story will be due for a big reset at some point in the not-so-distant future. Are the four hyperscalers really going to spend $993 billion on capex in 2027?” Jefferies questions. There are also important questions to ask about how much of the hyperscalers’ reported profits are down to their investments in AI model builders on which they will also depend for revenue. “Other income and expenses” — which describes gains in investments — have spiked in importance. Jefferies says these investments are “likely to include positions in unlisted AI-related stocks.” While the four major hyperscalers’ annualized earnings increased by $222 billion to reach $581 billion in the four quarters to 2Q26, “other non-operating income/loss” accounted for all of that increase, according to the analyst. Jefferies says “other non-operating income/loss” increased by $224 billion year-on-year to $237 billion over the same period, meaning it accounted "for all of the increase in earnings." Other research has underlined how much revenue and borrowing cloud providers might need to fund their datacenter building plans. The 2026 annual Global Technology Report from management consultants Bain & Company says the AI industry must generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding the infrastructure needed to meet anticipated demand. That means the industry will need new uses beyond employee productivity. Bain suspects existing AI applications might make up $1.8 trillion in revenue, but this still leaves a $4.2 trillion shortfall. It could be plugged by emerging AI applications such as search engines and ads, AI-built autonomous vehicles, and AI simulations. Even if they work out, these new categories will only add up to $1.5 trillion in revenue, leaving a $2.7 trillion gap which might be filled by “new products and uses that don’t exist today.” The Register does not offer investment advice.®

Beliau berkata, kelayakan bergantung kepada memenuhi syarat kemasukan akademik dan program khusus di empat institusi yang terlibat – Universiti Teknologi Swinburne Kampus Sarawak, Universiti Teknologi Sarawak (UTS), Universiti Curtin Malaysia, dan Kolej Universiti i-CATS.

“Mereka tidak perlu bahasa Melayu untuk layak masuk empat universiti kita atau menerima pendidikan tinggi percuma,” katanya pada sesi soal jawab di sidang Dewan Undangan Negeri (DUN) Sarawak.
Beliau menjawab soalan See Chee How (Bebas-Batu Lintang) berkait kriteria kelayakan pemegang UEC di bawah FTES.

Annuar berkata, syarat kemasukan adalah berbeza mengikut institusi dan program, yang mana pemegang UEC secara umumnya memerlukan lima Gred B untuk layak menyertai program ijazah sarjana muda, serta subjek prasyarat tambahan bagi kursus tertentu seperti matematik, matematik tambahan, dan sains fizikal. Sesetengah institusi turut menetapkan syarat penguasaan bahasa Inggeris mereka sendiri.
Pemegang UEC yang diterima masuk ke mana-mana daripada 64 kursus yang diliputi di bawah FTES tidak perlu mengemukakan permohonan berasingan bagi skim berkenaan.

Setakat 30 Jun lalu, seramai 192 pelajar UEC menerima pembiayaan yuran pengajian penuh di bawah FTES. Daripada jumlah tersebut, 137 pelajar menuntut di Swinburne Sarawak, 33 di UTS, 21 di Curtin Malaysia, dan seorang di Kolej Universiti i-CATS.
Annuar berkata, pelajar UEC akan menerima layanan sama seperti pelajar lain bagi penempatan latihan industri, tertakluk kejayaan mereka memperoleh penempatan dalam industri berkaitan.

Beliau berkata, penyertaan pemegang UEC dalam FTES mencerminkan dasar Sarawak untuk memastikan anak Sarawak yang layak mempunyai peluang saksama melanjutkan pengajian tinggi serta mengembangkan potensi, kemahiran, dan bakat.

Katanya, dasar pendidikan Sarawak berasaskan prinsip pendidikan seharusnya merentasi batas kaum dan etnik, bertindak sebagai wacana mobiliti sosial, selain membantu mengangkat komuniti keluar daripada belenggu kemiskinan – khususnya di kawasan luar bandar.
“Tiada anak Sarawak yang layak patut dinafikan peluang pendidikan,” katanya.
“Saya berharap ini menyampaikan mesej yang sangat jelas kepada seluruh rakyat Sarawak, terutamanya pemegang UEC, bahawa anda tidak ada bezanya dengan yang lain.”

38173097bce9c6a6: PETALING JAYA: Unified Examination Certificate (UEC) holders do not need to pass Bahasa Melayu to qualify for Sarawak’s Free Tertiary Education Scheme (FTES), says Sarawak’s deputy minister of education, innovation and talent development Dr Annuar Rapaee.

He said eligibility depended on meeting the academic and programme-specific admission requirements of the four participating institutions – Swinburne University of Technology Sarawak Campus, University of Technology Sarawak (UTS), Curtin University Malaysia and i-CATS University College.

According to The Borneo Post, he said UEC holders did not need to pass Bahasa Melayu to qualify for admission. However, he said they should be proficient in English as it is the main language of instruction at the four institutions.

“They do not need Bahasa Melayu to qualify for entry into our four universities or to receive free tertiary education,” he said during the question-and-answer session at the Sarawak state assembly sitting.
He was responding to See Chee How (Independent-Batu Lintang) about the eligibility criteria for UEC holders under FTES.

Annuar said admission requirements varied by institution and programme A UEC holder generally needs five Grade Bs to qualify for a bachelor’s degree programme, along with additional prerequisite subjects for certain courses such as Mathematics, Additional Mathematics and Physical Science. Some institutions also imposed their own English-language proficiency requirements.
UEC holders admitted to any of the 64 courses covered by FTES would not need to submit a separate application for the scheme.

As of June 30, 192 UEC students were receiving full tuition fee coverage under FTES. Of these, 137 were studying at Swinburne Sarawak, 33 at UTS, 21 at Curtin Malaysia and one at i-CATS University College.
Annuar said UEC students would receive the same treatment as other students in securing industrial placements, provided they obtained placements in the relevant industries.

He said the inclusion of UEC holders in FTES reflected Sarawak’s policy of ensuring that deserving Sarawakians had equal opportunities to pursue higher education and develop their potential, skills and talents.

He added that Sarawak’s education policy was based on the principle that education should transcend race and ethnicity, serve as a means of social mobility, and help lift communities out of poverty – particularly in rural areas.
“No deserving Sarawakian should be denied educational opportunities,” he said.
“I hope this sends a very clear message to all Sarawakians, particularly UEC holders, that you are no different from others.”

The UEC is the school-leaving certificate for students attending Chinese independent schools and is academically equivalent to the national Sijil Tinggi Persekolahan Malaysia (STPM) or international A-levels.
The certificate was recognised by Sarawak in 2016 for entry to state civil service positions, state-owned colleges and universities, and to qualify for Yayasan Sarawak education loans.

a2352b9071f96ed2: When it comes to deciding the fate of the planet, Colleen Golja always thought science and reason would have a seat at the table. That was until one morning last September in London, when the climate researcher took part in the first in a series of war games. The goal: to prevent an uncontrolled global race to develop a technology aimed at cooling the planet but that comes with vast, unknown risks that could reshape life on Earth.
“I thought that would be such an easy thing. Like, we can all agree to do ethical research and make sure it's for the better of all humans,” she told WIRED. “And boy, was I wrong.”

The simulation, titled Exploring Geopolitical Tipping Points and Climate Cooling Strategies, saw a couple dozen foreign-relations experts, scientists, military personnel, and former government officials from across the world convene in a meeting room at Queen Mary University of London. After making introductions over coffee and little yogurts, they sat at tables arranged in a square with the name of the country or organization each person was playing: national governments, climate NGOs and nonprofits, indigenous groups, and tech companies. Golja was assigned to provide technical advice to help participants make scientifically literate decisions.

23f8591ddbcecc53: OCTOBER 13 — Rare Earth Elements (REEs) are a group of 17 metallic elements which are found beneath the Earth’s surface in the Earth’s crust.
Accordingly, RREs constitute “land”. By definition, the word includes, among others, “the earth below the surface and all substances therein”. (See Section 3 of the National Land Code)
Land, in turn, is a state matter. (See Item 2 of the State List of the Ninth Schedule of the Federal Constitution).

More than a year ago in August, then Acting Minister of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability (NRES) Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani had explained that his ministry had no plans to establish a centralised body to regulate Malaysia’s REE industry.
Johari cited constitutional provisions — that is, the State List in the Ninth Schedule — as giving states authority over mining permits, leases and licences.

The minister also alluded to objections from state governments, saying several states had raised concerns during engagement sessions, viewing the proposal as an attempt to nationalise state-owned mineral resources.
Any move to centralise REE regulation therefore would require in-depth study and close consultation with all state governments to safeguard their rights.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

File picture for illustrative purposes only. The author says the proposed national entity for rare earth elements must not be seen as an attempt to nationalise state-owned mineral resources, as land matters fall under state jurisdiction. — Unsplash pic
Johari said so when winding up the 13th Malaysia Plan (13MP) debate for his ministry.

Petroleum resources are different. The Federal List in the Ninth Schedule includes Item 8 on “Trade, commerce and industry” which in turn includes “Development of mineral resources; mines, mining, minerals and mineral ores; oils and oilfields; purchase, sale, import and export of minerals and mineral ores; petroleum products; regulation of labour and safety in mines and oilfields” subject to Item 2(c) in the State List.
So, it is curious that Opposition Leader Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin should propose the establishment of a national entity to manage REE as a new source of national wealth in the post-petroleum era.

Hamzah said the entity — to be known as Reenas — was necessary to prevent non-radioactive raw materials worth more than RM800 billion from being sold cheaply without value-added processing or lost through illegal mining activities.
The intentions are good.
Five months ago, Professor Datuk Dr Ahmad Ibrahim wrote on REE as follows:

“Now, we face a new frontier: rare earths. The world is clamoring for them. They are the invisible heartbeat of electric vehicles, smartphones, and advanced defense systems. And here we sit, on potentially significant deposits. It is a second chance at industrial glory. But immediately, the scaremongers emerge. We hear the same words—radiation, thorium, danger—but this time they are amplified by a global network of non-governmental organizations and a sensationalist media. We must ask ourselves a hard question: Why?”
The reason may be in the famous saying: the road to hell is paved with good intentions.
It means that merely intending to do something good is not enough, and well-meaning actions can often lead to disastrous or harmful results.
Perhaps Johari was right: in-depth study and close consultation with all state governments to safeguard their rights are required.
That’s what federalism is all about.
If a centralised body to regulate Malaysia’s REE industry must not be seen as an attempt to nationalise state-owned mineral resources, what more a Petronas-like national entity on REE.
